etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English preien, from Anglo-Norman preier, from Old French preier, proier (French prier), from Latin precārī, from prex, precis (“a prayer, a request”), from Proto-Italic *preks, from Proto-Indo-European *preḱ- (“to ask, woo”).

Cognate via Indo-European of Old English frignan, fricgan, German fragen, Dutch vragen. Compare deprecate, imprecate, precarious.

definitions.definition: (religion) To direct words, thoughts, or one's attention to a deity or any higher being, for the sake of adoration, thanks, petition for help, etc.

quote.citation: 1905, Lord Dunsany [i.e., Edward Plunkett, 18th Baron of Dunsany], The Gods of Pegāna, London: [Charles] Elkin Mathews, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Pray to the small gods and hope that they may hear thee. Yet what mercy should the small gods have, who themselves made Death and Pain; or shall they restrain their old hound Time for thee?

quote.citation: 2021 January 13, Bethan McKernan, “Turkey drought: Istanbul could run out of water in 45 days”, in The Guardian‎[1]:
quote.text: The critically low level of rainfall in the second half of 2020 – approaching 50% year on year for November – led the religious affairs directorate to instruct imams and their congregations to pray for rain last month.

definitions.definition: To humbly beg a person for aid or their time.
(obsolete) To ask earnestly for; to seek to obtain by supplication; to entreat for.

quote.citation: 1598–1599 (first performance), William Shakespeare, “Much Adoe about Nothing”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene i]:
quote.text: I know not how to pray your patience.

definitions.definition: To wish or hope strongly for a particular outcome.
(obsolete) To implore, to entreat, to request.

quote.citation: 1596, Edmund Spenser, “Book VI, Canto IX”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC, stanza 7:
quote.text: They prayd him sit, and gave him for to feed  Such homely what as serves the simple clowne,  That doth despise the dainties of the towne […]

quote.citation: 1890, James George Frazer, The Golden Bough, volume 2, page 370:
quote.text: In time of drought the Abchases of the Caucasus sacrifice an ox to Ap-hi, the god of thunder and lightning, and an old man prays him to send rain, thunder, and lightning, telling him that the crops are parched.

quote.citation: 2021, Yang di-Pertuan Agong, “Schedule”, in Emergency (Essential Powers) (No. 2) Ordinance 2021‎[2], archived from the original on 20 July 2023, page 31:
quote.text: I humbly pray to the Honorable Court for the order for the removal of the publication which contains fake news to be granted.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Ellipsis of I pray you, I pray thee, whence also prithee.

definitions.definition: (archaic or formal) Please; used to make a polite request

quote.citation: 1815 December (indicated as 1816), [Jane Austen], chapter VIII, in Emma: […], volume I, London:  […]  [Charles Roworth and James Moyes] for John Murray, →OCLC, page 124:
quote.text: "Pray, Mr. Knightley," said Emma, who had been smiling to herself through a great part of this speech, "how do you know that Mr. Martin did not speak yesterday?"

quote.citation: 1840 April – 1841 November, Charles Dickens, “Chapter the Tenth”, in The Old Curiosity Shop. A Tale. […], volume I, London: Chapman and Hall, […], published 1841, →OCLC, page 144:
quote.text: Pray don’t ask me why, pray don’t be sorry, pray don’t be vexed with me, I have nothing to do with it indeed!

quote.citation: 1845, Frederick Marryat, “Chapter XXI”, in The Mission:
quote.text: Well, Major, pray tell us your adventures, for you have frightened us dreadfully.

quote.citation: 1892, Arthur Conan Doyle, The Adventure of the Engineer's Thumb:
quote.text: Thank you. I am sorry to have interrupted you. Pray continue your most interesting statement.

definitions.definition: Alternative form of pray tell (“I ask you (insincerely)”)

quote.citation: 20 September 2013, Martina Hyde, “Is the pope Catholic?”, in The Guardian‎[3]:
quote.text: He is a South American, so perhaps revolutionary spirit courses through Francis's veins. But what, pray, does the Catholic church want with doubt?
